prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- A Saudi Arabian blogger detained in December, ostensibly because he supported reform advocates accused by the Saudi government of backing terrorism, has been released, a fellow blogger posted Saturday. Web sites like this one pushed for Fouad al-Farhan's release. Ahmed al-Omran said on his blog, saudijeans.org, and later told CNN that he was awakened by a text message from the wife of Fouad al-Farhan, saying he had been released and was at home with his family. "That's great news, and this is just how I wanted to start my morning," al-Omran wrote. He said he later spoke with al-Farhan for several minutes on the telephone. "He sounded fine; he seems to be in good spirits," al-Omran said. "He said he would have more to talk about later but not at this point. He said now he'd like to take some time to spend with his family, with his children that he hasn't seen for so long."  Watch al-Omran describe his conversation with al-Farhan » . A Web site set up to call for al-Farhan's release said, "Fouad is free. He is back home in Jeddah after 137 days in custody." The Saudi Interior Ministry said it had no immediate comment on the reports. In January, a ministry spokesman said al-Farhan was arrested December 10 "because he violated the regulations of the kingdom." But in an e-mail posted on al-Farhan's Web site after his arrest, he told friends that he faced arrest for supporting 10 reform advocates the Saudi government accused of backing terrorism. In the e-mail, al-Farhan said a senior Interior Ministry official promised that he would remain in custody for three days at most if he agreed to sign a letter of apology. "I'm not sure if I'm ready to do that," he wrote. "An apology for what? Apologizing because I said the government is [a] liar when they accused those guys of supporting terrorism?" Al-Farhan, who blogs at alfarhan.org, is one of the few Saudi Web commentators to use his own name, according to the U.S.-based Committee to Protect Journalists. In January, the Bush administration expressed its concerns to the Saudi government regarding al-Farhan's detention at "a relatively senior level," U.S. State Department spokesman Sean McCormack said. "The U.S. stands for freedom of expression," McCormack said at the time. "Wherever people are seeking to express themselves, via the Internet or via other areas, whether in Saudi Arabia or elsewhere in the world, we stand with that freedom of expression, and that was our message to the Saudi government." The American Islamic Congress, a U.S.-based nonprofit organization, launched an online letter-writing campaign aimed at freeing al-Farhan, whom it called "the godfather of Saudi blogging." "All he did was express his opinions in a very obvious way, and he didn't threaten anyone," al-Omran said. "He was advocating against violence and terrorism." Al-Omran said al-Farhan had stopped blogging for a few months in late 2006, after the Interior Ministry ordered him to take down a blog he was operating, but he began again at a new site. He said al-Farhan told him he was treated well in jail. He also called al-Farhan's release a turning point for the blogging community in Saudi Arabia. "It showed the community of bloggers in Saudi Arabia can come together and support this cause -- support his freedom of speech -- even those who didn't agree with some of the things he wrote," he said. E-mail to a friend . CNN's Mohammed Jamjoom contributed to this report.

(CNN) — Fouad al-Farhan, a Saudi blogger who had been held since December—apparently over his support for reform activists whom Saudi authorities accused of aiding terrorism—has been freed, another blogger reported Saturday. Websites, including one created specifically for the campaign, had pressed for his release.

Ahmed al-Omran wrote on saudijeans.org, and later told CNN, that a text message from al-Farhan’s wife woke him with the news that her husband had been released and reunited with his family at home.

“This is wonderful news, and exactly how I wanted my morning to begin,” al-Omran wrote.

Al-Omran said he later had a brief telephone conversation with al-Farhan.

“He sounded well and appeared to be in good spirits,” al-Omran said. “He told me he would have more to say later, but not right now. For the moment, he wants to spend time with his family and with the children he has not seen in such a long time.”

Watch al-Omran discuss his conversation with al-Farhan.

A website established to campaign for the blogger’s freedom announced: “Fouad is free. After spending 137 days in detention, he has returned to his home in Jeddah.”

Saudi Arabia’s Interior Ministry did not immediately respond to the reports. In January, however, a ministry representative said al-Farhan had been taken into custody on December 10 for “violating the kingdom’s regulations.”

An email published on al-Farhan’s website after his arrest offered a different explanation. In it, he told friends that he expected to be detained because he had supported 10 reform campaigners accused by the Saudi government of backing terrorism.

Al-Farhan wrote that a high-ranking Interior Ministry official had assured him he would be held for no longer than three days if he signed an apology.

“I don’t know whether I am prepared to do that,” he wrote. “What would I be apologizing for? For saying the government was lying when it accused those men of supporting terrorism?”

According to the U.S.-based Committee to Protect Journalists, al-Farhan—whose blog is hosted at alfarhan.org—is among the small number of Saudi online commentators who publish under their real names.

In January, the Bush administration raised concerns about his detention with Saudi officials at “a relatively senior level,” State Department spokesman Sean McCormack said.

“The United States supports freedom of expression,” McCormack said at the time. “When people seek to voice their views—whether online or through other means, in Saudi Arabia or anywhere else—we support that right. That was the message we delivered to the Saudi government.”

The American Islamic Congress, a U.S.-based nonprofit group, also organized an online letter-writing effort seeking al-Farhan’s release. The organization described him as “the godfather of Saudi blogging.”

“He simply stated his views openly and did not threaten anybody,” al-Omran said. “He spoke out against both violence and terrorism.”

According to al-Omran, al-Farhan stopped blogging for several months toward the end of 2006 after the Interior Ministry instructed him to remove a blog he had been running. He subsequently resumed writing on a new website.

Al-Omran also said al-Farhan told him that prison officials had treated him well.

He described the release as a watershed moment for Saudi Arabia’s blogging community.

“It demonstrated that Saudi bloggers can unite behind a cause and defend his right to free expression, including people who disagreed with some of what he had written,” al-Omran said.

Email this story to a friend.

CNN’s Mohammed Jamjoom contributed to this report.

Al-Farhan, known for writing about political reform and social issues, was detained in Jeddah in December 2007. Saudi authorities said at the time that he was being questioned over alleged violations unrelated to state security, but they provided few details about his case.

Ahmed al-Omran, who writes the widely read *Saudi Jeans* blog, welcomed the release, describing it as happy news for Saudi Arabia’s online community and al-Farhan’s family. But al-Omran also said the detention had raised troubling questions because authorities never clearly explained why the blogger had been held for so long.

Al-Farhan’s case became a focal point for campaigners concerned about freedom of expression in the kingdom, where political activity is tightly restricted and journalists and bloggers can face detention or censorship for criticizing officials.

Human rights groups said his release was encouraging but warned that broader concerns remain. They called on Saudi authorities to clarify the legal basis for such detentions and to protect citizens who peacefully express their views online.

There was no immediate detailed statement from the Saudi government about the reasons for al-Farhan’s release.

# Saudi Arabia Releases Fouad al-Farhan, the “Godfather of Saudi Blogging”

**JEDDAH, Saudi Arabia —** Saudi authorities have released Fouad al-Farhan, one of the kingdom’s best-known online writers, after detaining him for more than four months without publicly charging him.

Al-Farhan, widely described as the “godfather of Saudi blogging” because of his early and influential role in the country’s online community, was freed on April 26, 2008. His release ended a 137-day detention that had drawn criticism from human-rights organizations, press-freedom groups, foreign governments and bloggers around the world.

The case became an important test of the limits of online political expression in Saudi Arabia. Although officials never announced formal charges, al-Farhan’s supporters said he was detained because of his writing about political reform, civil liberties and prisoners held without trial.

## Arrested after criticizing political detentions

Security officers arrested al-Farhan at his office in Jeddah on December 10, 2007. His family later said authorities searched both his office and home and confiscated computer equipment.

Shortly before his arrest, al-Farhan had warned friends that the Interior Ministry intended to question him. In an email circulated among other Saudi bloggers, he said an official had told him the authorities were concerned about his online advocacy on behalf of a group of detained reformists.

Those men—academics, lawyers and other public figures—had been arrested in February 2007. Saudi officials linked them to illegal fundraising and possible support for terrorism. Their supporters disputed that characterization, saying the detainees had been discussing peaceful political reform, including the creation of an independent civil-rights organization.

Al-Farhan had publicly called for their release and had described them as “prisoners of conscience.” He also wrote about government accountability, political participation and the need for greater openness in the kingdom.

Saudi authorities offered only a vague explanation for his detention. An Interior Ministry spokesman said al-Farhan was being questioned over violations of regulations unrelated to state security, but officials did not identify a specific law he was accused of breaking. He was never brought to a public trial.

That absence of a clear charge fueled suspicions that the detention was intended to punish or intimidate an increasingly prominent political blogger.

## A leading figure in Saudi Arabia’s emerging blogosphere

Al-Farhan’s importance extended beyond the size of his audience. At a time when Saudi newspapers and broadcasters operated under significant official constraints, blogs were beginning to provide a new forum for discussion of social and political issues.

Writing in Arabic under his own name, al-Farhan addressed subjects that many Saudis were reluctant to discuss publicly. His willingness to criticize indefinite detention and to identify himself openly made him a symbol of the kingdom’s nascent citizen-journalism movement.

Fellow bloggers therefore treated his arrest not as an isolated case but as a warning to the wider online community. They created “Free Fouad” websites and banners, circulated petitions, translated updates into several languages and coordinated online campaigns demanding information about his location and legal status.

His prolonged detention also illustrated the vulnerability of online writers in a system where authorities could hold suspects for extended periods with limited judicial scrutiny.

## International pressure for his release

Al-Farhan’s detention prompted responses from several international organizations.

The Committee to Protect Journalists called on Saudi authorities to release him and argued that his peaceful online commentary should not be treated as a criminal matter. Reporters Without Borders likewise condemned the detention and pressed the government to explain why he was being held.

Human Rights Watch said the case raised serious concerns about arbitrary detention and freedom of expression. Amnesty International treated al-Farhan as a prisoner of conscience, maintaining that he had been detained solely for peacefully expressing his views.

The United States also raised the case. State Department officials publicly expressed concern, sought information from Saudi authorities and emphasized that peaceful political expression should be protected.

The international campaign was reinforced by regional and global news coverage. For many observers outside Saudi Arabia, al-Farhan came to personify both the promise of blogging as an alternative public sphere and the risks faced by writers who challenged official narratives.

Saudi officials did not say whether that pressure played any role in the decision to free him. His release came without a trial, a public hearing or a detailed government statement resolving the reasons for his arrest.

## Solitary confinement, but no allegation of torture

After leaving prison, al-Farhan said he had spent a substantial portion of his detention in solitary confinement. He described isolation as the most difficult part of the experience and said he had been cut off from ordinary contact for weeks.

At the same time, he said he had not been tortured or physically abused. He reported that guards generally treated him properly and distinguished his experience from cases involving beatings or other forms of physical mistreatment.

His comments presented a nuanced picture: he did not accuse prison officials of torture, but he made clear that prolonged isolation and detention without charge had taken a psychological toll. Reports following his release said he had lost weight while in custody.

Al-Farhan also indicated that interrogators focused on his writings and political views. According to accounts of his detention, authorities wanted him to moderate or abandon his public activism. He reportedly resisted pressure to apologize for his writing or promise that he would stop blogging.

Despite that pressure, he emerged from prison saying he remained committed to reform and public discussion, though his immediate priority was to recover and spend time with his family.

## Release leaves central questions unanswered

Al-Farhan’s freedom was celebrated by his family, supporters and fellow bloggers, but the case ended without legal clarity. Authorities did not disclose the evidence against him, explain why he had been held for 137 days or say whether any restrictions had been placed on his future activities.

That uncertainty was central to the controversy. Human-rights advocates argued that even in the absence of physical abuse, holding a peaceful writer for months without charge or meaningful judicial review constituted a serious violation of his rights.

The episode also demonstrated the growing influence of online solidarity campaigns. Saudi bloggers, many of whom had never met al-Farhan, turned his detention into an international freedom-of-expression issue and kept his name in public view throughout his imprisonment.

His release was therefore welcomed as both a personal victory and a significant moment for Saudi Arabia’s digital public sphere. Yet it also underscored the narrow boundaries within which political speech operated: al-Farhan was free, but the state had shown that a blogger could still be detained for months without a public accusation.

For the writer known as the “godfather of Saudi blogging,” the end of imprisonment did not resolve the broader struggle over expression in the kingdom. It instead made that struggle more visible.
